newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Stokes says told by Howard no media deals.
newsitem.headline: Stokes says told by Howard no media deals.

text.p: Seven Network Ltd chairman Kerry Stokes said on Monday that he had been told by Australia's Prime Minister John Howard that he was not doing any deals which would affect the future of local media ownership.

Stokes criticised Howard last Friday, saying the Prime Minister had done a deal to deliver control of newspaper publisher John Fairfax Holdings Ltd to billionaire businessman Kerry Packer who already has a 15 percent stake in Fairfax and who owns the Nine Network, Seven's national television rival.

Howard confirmed the same day that he had discussed the future of local media ownership with News Corp Ltd executives which included discussions about News raising its stake in Seven from 14 percent at the moment in return for selling some Australian newspapers.

However, Howard rejected Stokes' claim that he had brokered a deal which would give Packer control of Nine and allow News Corp chairman Rupert Murdoch to take control of Seven by changing the media rules governing cross-media ownership, which applies to Packer, and foreign investment guidelines which apply to Murdoch as a United States citizen.
"I haven't backed down but I have spoken to Mr Howard. I accepted what he said to me," Stokes said in an interview on Seven's Today Tonight programme.
"There is not a deal being done and therefore I hope the Cabinet will look at this objectively rather than in an isolated instance," Stokes said.

"But I still object on my behalf of Seven, myself and all those shareholders to any discussion taking place regarding our shareholding in which we are not involved." Stokes is the largest shareholder in Seven, which ranks behind Nine in the national ratings, with 26 percent.
The programme said Cabinet was expected to consider planned changes to the media rules at a meeting in Canberra on Tuesday.

Packer's Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd is the largest shareholder in Fairfax behind Brierley Investments ltd of New Zealand, which has 20 percent but is prevented by foreign investment rules from holding more than 25 percent.
Fairfax shares ended two cents higher at A$3.25 on Monday after reaching a 12-month high of A$3.30 on market talk that Packer was on the verge of launching a cash and scrip bid.
The takeover talk gained currency on Saturday when Packer cancelled a deal to buy control of Sydney Harbour Casino Ltd, citing new strategic objectives which he did not identify.
Fairfax, publisher of the Sydney Morning Herald, Melbourne Age and Australian Financial Review dailies, is valued at A$2.47 billion at current market prices.
